procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 22nd November 1952 of the Judicial Commissioner's Court, Ajmer, in Misc. Petition No. 226 of 1952, refusing to issue a writ directing the authorities to permit the appellant to hold his fair.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant applied to the Judicial Commissioner's Court at Ajmer for a writ to permit him to hold his fair. He argued that his fundamental rights were infringed and that the rules promulgated by the Chief Commissioner were ultra vires the Regulation under which he purported to act. The Judicial Commissioner refused to issue the writ but granted leave to appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 132(1) of the Constitution.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court under Article 132(1) of the Constitution of India from the Judgment and Order of the Judicial Commissioner's Court, Ajmer. The leave granted by the Judicial Commissioner was confined to the vires of the Regulation and the bye-laws, but the Supreme Court allowed the appellant to attack the validity of the District Magistrate's action as well.

issue.issue_text: Whether the rules requiring a permit from the District Magistrate to hold a fair are beyond the scope of the rule-making power conferred by sections 40 and 41 of the Ajmer Laws Regulation, 1877.

facts: Under the Ajmer Laws Regulation of 1877, the Chief Commissioner was empowered to make rules to establish a proper system of conservancy and sanitation at fairs.
The Chief Commissioner framed rules that prohibited holding a fair without a permit from the District Magistrate.

These rules required the District Magistrate to be satisfied that the applicant could establish a proper system of sanitation and also empowered him to revoke a permit at any time without giving reasons or notice.
law: Section 40 of the Ajmer Laws Regulation, 1877, grants the Chief Commissioner the power to make rules "for the establishment of a proper system of conservancy and sanitation at fairs".
application: The Court determined that the Regulation gave the power to create a "system" of sanitation to the Chief Commissioner, not the District Magistrate. The rules, however, did not establish a system themselves.

Instead, the rules improperly delegated the authority to the District Magistrate to determine what a "proper system" was on a case-by-case basis. The Court found this delegation of power to be unauthorized and therefore *ultra vires* (beyond the legal power).
Furthermore, the rule allowing the District Magistrate to revoke a permit "without assigning any reasons or giving any previous notice" was deemed an "absolute and arbitrary power."
The Court reasoned that the Regulation's purpose was to ensure sanitation, not to give an official the power to arbitrarily prohibit the holding of fairs, which is a constitutionally protected right.

The net effect of the rules was to create a system of *ad hoc* control by the District Magistrate, which was not what the law intended when it authorized the creation of a system of conservancy and sanitation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the argument, holding that the rules were *ultra vires* the Ajmer Laws Regulation. The rules improperly delegated the Chief Commissioner's rule-making power to the District Magistrate and created an arbitrary system of control that went beyond the scope of establishing a system for sanitation as authorized by the law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the regulation and the bye-laws framed thereunder amount to an unreasonable restriction on the appellant's fundamental right to hold a cattle fair on his own land under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.

facts: The appellant, an Istimrardar, had been holding a cattle fair on his own land for about twenty years.
The Chief Commissioner of Ajmer, under the Ajmer Laws Regulation of 1877, framed rules requiring a permit from the District Magistrate to hold a fair.
The appellant applied for a permit but was refused on the ground that permits would no longer be issued to private individuals, only to local bodies.
law: Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution guarantees the fundamental right to engage in an occupation or business, which includes holding a fair.
Section 40 of the Ajmer Laws Regulation of 1877 empowers the Chief Commissioner to make rules for establishing a "proper system of conservancy and sanitation at fairs."
application: The Court determined that the rules framed by the Chief Commissioner were 'ultra vires' (beyond the power granted by) the Ajmer Laws Regulation for two main reasons.

First, the Regulation empowered the Chief Commissioner to establish a system of sanitation. However, the rules improperly delegated this authority to the District Magistrate by allowing him to decide what a "proper system" is. The Court held that the Chief Commissioner could not delegate this legislative power.

Second, a rule allowing the District Magistrate to revoke a permit "without assigning any reasons or giving any previous notice" was deemed to grant an absolute and arbitrary power. The Court found this unacceptable, as the Chief Commissioner cannot authorize a subordinate to arbitrarily prohibit a constitutionally guaranteed right.
The Court also noted that the District Magistrate's specific reason for refusal (a policy against private individuals) was not authorized even by the (invalid) rules themselves.
Because the rules were found to be invalid on the grounds of being 'ultra vires' the parent Regulation, the District Magistrate's order based on those rules was also invalid.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's position. It held that the rules under which the permit was denied were invalid because they went beyond the powers granted by the parent legislation (the Ajmer Laws Regulation). The rules improperly delegated legislative authority to the District Magistrate and gave him arbitrary power. Since the rules were invalid, the Court allowed the appeal without needing to explicitly decide the constitutional question of whether they constituted an unreasonable restriction under Article 19.

issue.issue_text: Whether the District Magistrate's action in refusing the permit to hold the fair was valid.

facts: The appellant, a private individual, applied for a permit to hold a cattle fair on his own land.
The District Magistrate refused the permit, stating that as a matter of policy, permits would only be issued to local bodies and not to private individuals.
law: The Ajmer Laws Regulation of 1877 empowers the Chief Commissioner to make rules "for the establishment of a proper system of conservancy and sanitation at fairs."

The rules framed under this Regulation required a permit from the District Magistrate to hold a fair and empowered him to satisfy himself that the applicant could establish a proper system of sanitation and security.
application: The Court found the District Magistrate's refusal was invalid for two main reasons.

First, the Magistrate's reason for refusal (that the applicant was a private individual) was not a ground authorized by the rules. The rules only allowed him to assess the applicant's ability to manage sanitation and security.
Second, and more fundamentally, the Court held that the rules themselves were invalid and 'ultra vires' (beyond the power of the authority that made them).

The rules were invalid because the law required the Chief Commissioner to create a "system" of sanitation in the rules themselves. Instead, the rules improperly delegated this power to the District Magistrate, allowing him to decide what a "proper system" was on an ad hoc basis.
Furthermore, the rules gave the District Magistrate an absolute and arbitrary power to revoke permits without reason, which was also deemed 'ultra vires'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the validity of the District Magistrate's action. Since the Magistrate acted on a ground not permitted by the rules, and because the rules themselves were invalid for improperly delegating power and being arbitrary, his order refusing the permit was bad in law.

cases.case_name: Tahir Hussain v. District Board, Muzafarnagar
cases.principle: This case was referred to in the concurring opinion to support the conclusion that the rules made were not within the intendment of the section which authorised the making of the rules, as they established a system of ad hoc control by the District Magistrate rather than a system of conservancy and sanitation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A rule-making authority, empowered by a statute to establish a specific system, acts beyond its powers (ultra vires) if it delegates the substantive function of defining that system to a subordinate official. Furthermore, rules are ultra vires if they confer absolute, arbitrary, and uncontrolled power upon a subordinate official to prohibit a legally or constitutionally protected right.
obiter: It is not necessary to express an opinion as to whether the impugned order also infringes the appellant's fundamental rights under article 19.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The rules framed by the Chief Commissioner are ultra vires the Ajmer Laws Regulation, 1877. The Regulation empowers the Chief Commissioner to make rules that themselves establish a system of conservancy and sanitation, but instead, he created rules that improperly delegated this power to the District Magistrate, allowing the Magistrate to determine the system on an ad hoc basis. Furthermore, the rules unconstitutionally grant the District Magistrate an absolute and arbitrary power to revoke permits without reason, which is an invalid prohibition on the guaranteed right to hold a fair. Consequently, the District Magistrate's order refusing the permit, being based on these invalid rules, is void.
legal_tests_applied: Ultra Vires Doctrine: The court assessed whether the rules exceeded the scope of the rule-making authority conferred by the parent statute (sections 40 and 41 of the Ajmer Laws Regulation, 1877), concluding that the creation of a system of 'ad hoc control' by a magistrate was not within the intendment of the section.

Improper Delegation Doctrine: The court determined that the Chief Commissioner, who was granted the power to frame the rules for a sanitation system, could not delegate that legislative authority to the District Magistrate to determine what a 'proper system' is.

Arbitrariness as an Unreasonable Restriction: The court found that a rule empowering the District Magistrate to revoke a permit 'without assigning any reasons or giving any previous notice' constitutes an 'absolute and arbitrary power uncontrolled by any discretion' that unlawfully prohibits a constitutionally guaranteed right.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning reinforces the principle that a regulating law must itself establish the system of regulation, so that citizens can know what is required of them and comply. The power to regulate cannot be an unfettered, ad hoc power left to the discretion of an executive officer.

The ruling protects the fundamental right to conduct a business from arbitrary executive prohibition. The court states that the Chief Commissioner cannot 'invest the District Magistrate with the right arbitrarily to prohibit that which the law and the Constitution, not only allow, but guarantee.'
